The Fat Cantor Set

This scene builds the fat Cantor set. Dig out only a little at each stage, and half the length survives.

Digging less changes the outcome. The remaining set is still full of holes, with empty interior. Yet its length converges to one half. Size by length and size by topology are independent.

For example, scoop a 🍰 cake again, but take only small bites. Holes appear everywhere, yet half the cake remains to eat. It looks empty, but the amount is real.

Show proof

  1. Feasibility check: let ℓn\ell_nℓn​ be the common length of the stage-nnn intervals; then ℓ0=1\ell_0 = 1ℓ0​=1 and ℓn=(ℓn−1−4−n)/2\ell_n = (\ell_{n-1} - 4^{-n})/2ℓn​=(ℓn−1​−4−n)/2.

    Induction gives the exact formula ℓn=2−n+4−n2\ell_n = \frac{2^{-n} + 4^{-n}}{2}ℓn​=22−n+4−n​ (n=0n = 0n=0: 1+12=1\frac{1 + 1}{2} = 121+1​=1; the step is a direct substitution).

    Hence ℓn−1=2−(n−1)+4−(n−1)2>2−(n−1)2=2−n>4−n\ell_{n-1} = \frac{2^{-(n-1)} + 4^{-(n-1)}}{2} > \frac{2^{-(n-1)}}{2} = 2^{-n} > 4^{-n}ℓn−1​=22−(n−1)+4−(n−1)​>22−(n−1)​=2−n>4−n for n≥1n \ge 1n≥1, so a middle interval of length 4−n4^{-n}4−n genuinely fits — the removal is possible at every stage.

  2. At stage nnn there are 2n−12^{n-1}2n−1 surviving closed intervals from stage n−1n-1n−1, and exactly one middle open interval of length 4−n4^{-n}4−n is removed from each.

    Removed open intervals from different stages and different parent intervals are all pairwise disjoint (each is carved out of the interior of a closed interval, and the surviving sets are nested).

    So the total length removed through stage NNN is the sum of the per-stage contributions.

  3. The stage-nnn contribution is 2n−1⋅4−n2^{n-1} \cdot 4^{-n}2n−1⋅4−n.

    Simplifying the exponent, 2n−14n=2n−122n=2−n−1\dfrac{2^{n-1}}{4^n} = \dfrac{2^{n-1}}{2^{2n}} = 2^{-n-1}4n2n−1​=22n2n−1​=2−n−1, so the total removed length is the geometric series ∑n=1∞2−n−1\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 2^{-n-1}∑n=1∞​2−n−1 with ratio 12\tfrac1221​.

    Its first term is 14\tfrac1441​, giving 1/41−1/2=12\dfrac{1/4}{1 - 1/2} = \tfrac121−1/21/4​=21​.

  4. The finite-stage version: through stage NNN the total removed is the partial sum ∑n=1N2−n−1=14⋅1−2−N1−1/2=12(1−2−N)\sum_{n=1}^{N} 2^{-n-1} = \tfrac14 \cdot \dfrac{1 - 2^{-N}}{1 - 1/2} = \tfrac12(1 - 2^{-N})∑n=1N​2−n−1=41​⋅1−1/21−2−N​=21​(1−2−N).

    Starting from [0,1][0,1][0,1], the length remaining after NNN stages is 1−12(1−2−N)=12(1+2−N)1 - \tfrac12(1 - 2^{-N}) = \tfrac12(1 + 2^{-N})1−21​(1−2−N)=21​(1+2−N), tending to 12\tfrac1221​ as N→∞N \to \inftyN→∞.

    For N=1N = 1N=1 this is 1−14=34=12(1+12)1 - \tfrac14 = \tfrac34 = \tfrac12(1 + \tfrac12)1−41​=43​=21​(1+21​) — the surviving intervals [ 0,38 ][\,0, \tfrac38\,][0,83​] and [ 58,1 ][\,\tfrac58, 1\,][85​,1] with the middle (38,58)(\tfrac38, \tfrac58)(83​,85​) carved out, exactly as the scene shows.

Passing from the finite partial sums to the infinite total uses countable additivity of Lebesgue measure (continuity from below): for the pairwise-disjoint union GGG of the removed intervals, m(G)=∑n=1∞2n−14−n=lim⁡N→∞∑n=1N2−n−1=12m(G) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 2^{n-1} 4^{-n} = \lim_{N \to \infty} \sum_{n=1}^{N} 2^{-n-1} = \tfrac12m(G)=∑n=1∞​2n−14−n=limN→∞​∑n=1N​2−n−1=21​.

    Hence the pairwise-disjoint union GGG of the removed open intervals has Lebesgue measure m(G)=12m(G) = \tfrac12m(G)=21​, and since C=[0,1]∖GC = [0,1] \setminus GC=[0,1]∖G, we get m(C)=1−12=12>0m(C) = 1 - \tfrac12 = \tfrac12 > 0m(C)=1−21​=21​>0.

    This is where the fat Cantor set parts company with the standard Cantor set (middle third removed each stage, remaining length (2/3)n→0(2/3)^n \to 0(2/3)n→0).

Let U=[0,1]∖CU = [0,1] \setminus CU=[0,1]∖C be the complement of the fat Cantor set.

Prove UUU is (relatively) open, dense in [0,1][0,1][0,1], and has m(U)=12m(U) = \tfrac12m(U)=21​.

Then finish by completing this table: "empty interior, yet half the length" — measure and topological size are independent notions.

U=⋃stages(removed open intervals)U = \bigcup_{\text{stages}} \text{(removed open intervals)}U=stages⋃​(removed open intervals)
m(U)=12,m(C)=12m(U) = \tfrac12,\quad m(C) = \tfrac12m(U)=21​,m(C)=21​
m=0m>0nowhere densestandard Cantorfat CantordenseQ∩[0,1]irrationals in [0,1]\begin{array}{c|cc} & m = 0 & m > 0 \\ \hline \text{nowhere dense} & \text{standard Cantor} & \textbf{fat Cantor} \\ \text{dense} & \mathbb{Q} \cap [0,1] & \text{irrationals in } [0,1] \end{array}nowhere densedense​m=0standard CantorQ∩[0,1]​m>0fat Cantorirrationals in [0,1]​​
Show proof

  1. UUU is the complement of the closed set CCC, hence relatively open in [0,1][0,1][0,1]. Concretely, UUU is the union of the removed open intervals over all stages — a countable union of pairwise-disjoint open intervals.

  2. Dense: the previous problem showed that every nonempty open interval meets a removed open interval.

    Handle the relative topology as well: a nonempty relatively open subset of [0,1][0,1][0,1] contains either an open interval or an endpoint-touching piece [0,a)[0, a)[0,a) with a>0a > 0a>0 or (b,1](b, 1](b,1] with b<1b < 1b<1.

    In the endpoint cases it still contains a nonempty open interval, namely (0,a)(0, a)(0,a) or (b,1)(b, 1)(b,1), so the previous argument applies verbatim.

    Hence every relatively open set contains a point of UUU, so UUU is dense in [0,1][0,1][0,1].

  3. Measure: the removed open intervals are pairwise disjoint, so m(U)=∑n=1∞2n−14−n=12m(U) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} 2^{n-1} 4^{-n} = \tfrac12m(U)=∑n=1∞​2n−14−n=21​ (the geometric series from the first problem). Hence m(C)=m([0,1])−m(U)=1−12=12m(C) = m([0,1]) - m(U) = 1 - \tfrac12 = \tfrac12m(C)=m([0,1])−m(U)=1−21​=21​.

  4. To summarize: CCC is closed, has empty interior (nowhere dense), is perfect, and has length 12\tfrac1221​; its complement UUU is open, dense, and has length 12\tfrac1221​.

    The table above fills all four cells — the standard Cantor set (nowhere dense, measure 0), the fat Cantor set (nowhere dense, measure 12\tfrac1221​), the rationals in [0,1][0,1][0,1] (dense, measure 0), the irrationals (dense, measure 1).

    There are even sets that are open and dense with arbitrarily small measure (enumerate the rationals as q1,q2,…q_1, q_2, \dotsq1​,q2​,… — the index starts at k≥1k \ge 1k≥1 — and around each qkq_kqk​ take an open interval of radius ε/2k\varepsilon/2^kε/2k: each interval has length 2ε/2k2\varepsilon/2^k2ε/2k, and ∑k=1∞2ε/2k=2ε\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} 2\varepsilon/2^k = 2\varepsilon∑k=1∞​2ε/2k=2ε, so the total measure is ≤2ε\le 2\varepsilon≤2ε).

    The punchline: the topological statement "has empty interior" and the measure-theoretic statement "has such-and-such length" impose nothing on each other — and the fat Cantor set is the most dramatic witness to their independence.
